items.question: How is TypeScript different from JavaScript at run time?
items.answer: TypeScript is not a separate run-time language. The TypeScript compiler (tsc) checks your code, strips all type syntax, and emits plain JavaScript. Browsers and Node.js execute that JavaScript on an engine like V8. Interfaces, type aliases, and generic parameters never exist at run time — only values, functions, and emitted constructs like classes or enums remain.

items.sixtySeconds: TS checks then erases. JS runs on V8. No interface tags at run time. Validate JSON at boundaries.

items.question: How does TypeScript compare to C# for typing?
items.answer: Both offer static analysis, but C# compiles to Intermediate Language (IL) with type metadata the Common Language Runtime (CLR) enforces at run time. TypeScript types are erasable — they help during development and CI but do not change how JavaScript behaves. A C# DTO deserialized from JSON is a real CLR type; a TypeScript interface on JSON.parse is a compile-time assertion only unless you add runtime validation.
followUps: When do you need OpenAPI between Node and .NET?
What does Roslyn emit that tsc does not?
items.sixtySeconds: C# keeps types in IL. TS erases to JS. CLR enforces; TS does not. Polyglot needs schema.

items.question: Walk through the TypeScript compile pipeline.
items.answer: Source .ts files are parsed into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST). The type checker validates assignments, calls, and strict flags. On success, tsc transforms the AST — erasing types and optionally downleveling syntax — then emits .js files, optional .d.ts declarations, and source maps. A bundler may then package output for deployment. Node or the browser executes the final JavaScript.
followUps: Why do teams use tsc --noEmit with Vite?
items.sixtySeconds: Parse → check → erase → emit JS. CI often --noEmit. Bundle optional. Not IL like C#.

items.question: What belongs in tsconfig.json for a strict new project?
items.answer: Enable strict: true (which turns on strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, and related flags). Set target and module appropriately — NodeNext for Node ESM libraries. Define include/exclude globs, outDir, and rootDir. For monorepos, use composite: true on libraries and references for tsc -b incremental builds. skipLibCheck speeds CI; forceConsistentCasingInFileNames prevents cross-platform import bugs.
followUps: When use moduleResolution bundler vs NodeNext?
items.sixtySeconds: strict true. NodeNext for Node ESM. include/outDir. references for monorepos. paths needs bundler too.

items.question: What are erasable types, and what survives at run time?
items.answer: Erasable types are TypeScript-only constructs removed during emit: interfaces, type aliases, import type, and generic parameters. Classes, functions, and variables emit as JavaScript. Enums are a special case — they generate a run-time object. You cannot instanceof an interface. For external data, use unknown plus narrowing or a schema validator — compile-time types do not protect run time.
followUps: Why do some teams avoid enum?
items.sixtySeconds: Interfaces erase. Classes emit. Generics erase. Enums emit object. Validate API boundaries.

items.question: When should you annotate types explicitly versus relying on inference?
items.answer: Annotate parameters and return types on exported functions and public APIs so consumers get stable .d.ts contracts. Let locals infer when initializers are clear — const count = 0 does not need : number. Annotate empty arrays (const items: Order[] = []) to avoid never[]. Use unknown at boundaries, not any. C# always declares member types; TypeScript prefers inference inside function bodies.
followUps: Why does let widen string literals?
items.sixtySeconds: Annotate exports. Infer locals. unknown at edges. Empty array needs type hint.

items.question: How do you adopt TypeScript in a large JavaScript codebase?
items.answer: Add tsconfig with allowJs to include existing .js files. Rename high-churn modules to .ts over time. Install @types/* for npm dependencies or write minimal .d.ts shims. Enable checkJs with JSDoc for files you have not renamed. Tighten strict per folder as migration progresses. Avoid permanent @ts-ignore — use // @ts-expect-error with a plan. C# integration stays at HTTP/JSON boundaries with OpenAPI, not mixed compilation.
followUps: What is a declare module block?
items.sixtySeconds: allowJs migrate. @types or .d.ts shims. strict per folder. C# via OpenAPI not allowJs.

items.question: Your CI passes but production throws TypeError on API data — what went wrong?
items.answer: TypeScript only caught compile-time assumptions. JSON.parse returns any/unknown shapes — assigning to a typed variable without validation is a lie after erasure. The API may have changed, or the backend (perhaps C#) serializes differently than the front-end interface expects. Fix: parse with Zod or similar at the boundary, use unknown, and align contracts with OpenAPI or JSON Schema across services.
followUps: How is this different from C# deserialization errors?
When would you codegen types from OpenAPI?
items.sixtySeconds: TS types erased. JSON untrusted. Validate at boundary. Schema sync with .NET API.

items.question: Why is tsc not the same as dotnet build?
items.answer: dotnet build invokes Roslyn to emit IL assemblies with preserved type metadata for the CLR. tsc emits JavaScript without type metadata for JavaScript engines. tsc can type-check without emitting (--noEmit). dotnet build always produces assemblies (unless analyzers-only scenarios). Deployment artifacts differ: .dll versus .js bundle. Type safety guarantees differ: CLR run-time enforcement versus compile-time-only for TypeScript.
items.sixtySeconds: dotnet → IL + CLR types. tsc → JS, types gone. Different hosts, artifacts, run-time safety.
